Bethel
BETH-el
noun (place)
From the Hebrew Beyth-'El, “house of God,” from bayith (house) and 'El (God).

See also: Bethel · Bethel

📖 Biblical Definition

Bethel means “house of God,” the name Jacob gave to the place where, fleeing Esau, he saw in a dream a ladder set up on the earth whose top reached to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the LORD standing above it renewing the covenant promise (Gen 28:10-22). Awaking, Jacob confessed, “Surely the LORD is in this place,” anointed the stone of his pillow, and vowed. Our Lord Himself unveils the ladder's meaning, declaring that He is the way between heaven and earth, the true Bethel where God and man meet (John 1:51). Bethel thus stands as a type of Christ, the one mediator and the living house of God. Yet the place became a parable of how true worship is debased into idolatry, for Jeroboam, fearing the pull of Jerusalem, set up a golden calf at Bethel and another at Dan, ordained unauthorized priests, and devised a feast out of his own heart (1 Kgs 12:28-33). The house of God was made a house of calves. Bethel therefore teaches a double lesson: where God meets His people there is grace and a ladder to heaven, but where men invent their own worship the holiest name becomes a shrine of sin. The remedy is to worship only as God has commanded, through the Mediator He has appointed.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

“House of God”; the place of Jacob's ladder and vow, later seat of Jeroboam's calf-worship.

expand to see more

BETHEL, noun (place). From the Hebrew bayith, house, and 'El, God; the house of God.

A place in the hill country of Ephraim, originally called Luz, renamed by Jacob.

The site of Jacob's vision of a ladder reaching to heaven and of his solemn vow.

Later one of the two royal shrines where Jeroboam set a golden calf: “And he set the one in Bethel, and the other put he in Dan.” (1 Kgs 12:29)

Figuratively, a place where God is present and worshipped—or, when corrupted, a monument to false worship.

📖 Key Scripture

Gen 28:17 — "And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."

Gen 28:19 — "And he called the name of that place Bethel: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first."

1Ki 12:28 — "Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt."

Amo 5:5 — "But seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and pass not to Beersheba: for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nought."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The chief danger is the ancient one Bethel itself displays—will-worship dressed in the name of God—rather than a modern academic redefinition.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Bethel's warning is timeless: Jeroboam did not deny God but reinvented His worship for convenience, and the same impulse animates every age that prefers worship devised “out of his own heart” to worship commanded in Scripture. The principle to recover is the regulative pattern—that God is to be worshipped in the way He has appointed, not in ways men find expedient or pleasing.

The recovery is reverent obedience. The same place that was once the gate of heaven became a snare because men kept the holy name while abandoning the holy command. Bethel thus presses upon the church the abiding rule that nearness to God is found only through His appointed Mediator and His appointed means, never through golden substitutes of our own making.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Bethel is a transparent Hebrew compound naming a dwelling of deity.

expand to see more

bayith — house, dwelling, household; the common Hebrew word for home.

'El — God, the strong One; the ancient Semitic name for deity.

Together Beyth-'El — “house of God,” the very gate of heaven.

The earlier name of the city was Luz, meaning almond or hazel.

The contrasting shrine-name Beth-aven, “house of vanity,” was later flung at corrupted Bethel by the prophets.

Usage

"Of the literal city and sanctuary in the hill country of Ephraim."

"Of the place of Jacob's ladder, taken as a type of Christ the mediator."

"Of the corrupted shrine of Jeroboam's calf-worship, a byword for false religion."
